#1006. Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous

It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it.

The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?

This year clubs from the south coast to the north-east have reported disorder caused by supporters under the age of 18, some seemingly as young as 10. In February, Aldershot Town experienced a series of disorderly incidents involving young people that included brawls outside the ground, behaviour the club described as “wholly unacceptable and [which] will not be tolerated”. In August, Enfield Town said they were “concerned and disappointed” by young fans at a fixture in Lewes. Two weeks ago, a Gloucester City fan was hit by a rock thrown by teenagers at Redditch United during an FA Trophy tie. Even Soham Town Rangers of the ninth-tier Eastern Counties League urged parents to ensure their children make “sensible choices” ahead of a match against Mildenhall Town.

Hednesford have experienced consistent trouble for a number of seasons and in August their owner and chair, Craig Gwilt, attempted to face it down. A rising tide of disorder was harming the club, he said, behaviour that included “pitch invasions, fighting, abuse directed towards players, missiles being thrown at opposition goalkeepers, flares entering the field of play and even interference with players’ water bottles”. He called on fans to improve their behaviour or risk permanently damaging the club. The plea was not immediately heard. Three weeks after Gwilt’s statement the club banned 20 young supporters from attending matches after there was action away at Telford.

Hednesford is a town of 19,000 people on the edge of the protected landscape of Cannock Chase. The town centre is neat and tidy, a well-maintained monument to the Stafford regiment at its heart. On the way to the ground you can get a pint at the Cross Keys where Dick Turpin reputedly rested his head. It’s a town seemingly at peace with itself and the club is at the heart of the community. But both are struggling to get to grips with an issue that leaves people scratching their heads.

This season the club have introduced measures to prevent under-16s from entering without an accompanying adult. There is also extra security on matchdays, ostensibly to manage car parking. These interventions appear to have contained any trouble in and around the stadium, but now gangs of up to 50 youths will gather post-match at a safe remove to look for trouble or, more likely, save their energy for an away fixture. Like the one at Chester, for example, when the schooligans were removed from one train for antisocial behaviour and were drinking alcohol throughout their journey up. Encountering such groups on a Saturday will be familiar to many rail passengers.

The schooligans, whose nickname was coined by Hednesford’s security staff, “baffle” the club’s chief executive, Marvin Robinson, who would rather be spending his time modernising a club that have had back-to-back promotions. “I’m not really sure I understand why it seems to be a trend,” he says. “It’s a wider social issue but what is it and what will it become? Is it a social media thing? Is it about notoriety or becoming known for something? The adult response online has been almost to normalise it. I don’t agree with that.”

Go on TikTok and the picture does start to become a little clearer. From aggregator accounts to individual semi-anonymised accounts belonging to the teenagers, there is a wealth of posts celebrating the behaviour of “top lads” who “mooch” to the ground before “running” the opposition out of town. Often set to a backing of euphoric electronic dance music with a layer or two of visual effects and captions such as “this weekend’s got me feeling like a little kid at Christmas”, the posts are celebratory and almost nostalgic in tone. In recent weeks TikTok has begun appending disclaimers to them that read: “Participating in this activity could result in you or others getting hurt.” TikTok removed an account named “NLN [National League North] gimps and chants”, when alerted to it by the Guardian, for contravening guidelines that do not allow content that glorifies violence.

The mythology of old-school football hooliganism appears to be well‑known among these groups, with references to the 2005 film Green Street commonplace. But the schooligans of 2026 don’t behave like the firms of the past. For a start they rarely, if at all, arrange to fight their rivals. Instead they use the mapping feature on Snapchat to alert opposition to their presence on the day, and take it from there. The concept of rivalry itself is fluid. In the West Midlands, for example, teens from Hednesford will band together with those nominally affiliated with Redditch or Cannock Town. When there was trouble recently at Hednesford’s fixture at Hereford, local police said the majority of disorder had been caused by Redditch fans chasing supporters from Solihull Moors. It isn’t just local either. Children as young as 12 have been detained in the north-west having travelled from the south coast, a distance of more than 200 miles.

The chair of Redditch, David Faulkner, is still dealing with the fallout from the Gloucester tie two weeks ago. He says the fluid set of alliances between ultra groups has created a “travelling circus” and that no one knows where it will turn up next. Branding himself “the non-League chair”, Faulkner has started posting videos on YouTube drawing attention to the disorder and calling for collective action.

“People think of non-league football as one man and his dog, but we need to catch up with the fact that it’s massive now,” Faulkner says. “Some clubs have attendances bigger than in League One but the regulations were put in place decades ago. We need that extra regulation, that support, so we can get the funding to put things like CCTV and more stewarding in place. Because the other way this could go is that [change only happens] when someone gets seriously hurt. I haven’t got metal detectors on our gates to stop kids bringing knives in. None of that stuff. I’d rather take action before something happens.”

The Football Association says the behaviour of fans is primarily a matter for clubs and relevant authorities but that it is working to develop policies that welcome young fans safely to National League grounds. The UK Football Policing Unit, meanwhile, is working alongside leagues and the Crown Prosecution Service to develop new policies around “youth risk”, which are likely to include an extra focus on education via schools and community work.

“It’s probably the most important area of football policing that we’re focused on,” says Mike Ankers, the deputy director of the UKFPU. “We are seeing children as young as 12 or 13 engaged in antisocial behaviour at best, but also actual violence and that’s up and down the country, with some travelling hundreds of miles. There comes a great risk and a great safeguarding issue with regards to that. In terms of our focus, we are making sure that we bring the right people together to have a solution. It’s not just the policing, it requires a more holistic view.”

Ankers says he supports Faulkner in speaking up on the topic and believes many more adults need to take responsibility. “These children need a strong adult role model,” he says. “I would very much question that if your 12-year-old is going out to follow football and is being detained, perhaps 200 miles away, then you need to look at how they’ve been able to travel and have those conversations. I think there’s very much a role for parental responsibility.”

The Hednesford schooligans, having been deposited on the platform at Chester by police, made their way home by train, only to find themselves stuck in a combination of Halloween revellers and national signal failure. Constrained, they hunched over their phones viewing footage from different teenage firms and discussed the day’s events. In the end, they concurred they had got the best of it. After all, said one: “What experience do you get from chasing a taxi?”

TikTok and Snapchat were approached for comment.

#1004. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

Manchester United could finally hire Mauricio Pochettino a decade after Sir Alex Ferguson endorsed the Argentine manager due to his commitment to young players.

"He understands the advantage of playing young people. They won't let you down and they have been fantastic."

Pochettino previously met Ferguson for lunch in London and have had a friendly relationship since their time at League Managers Association dinners.

#999. Graham Potter on his Swedish love affair, Viktor Gyokeres and World Cup pain: ‘You’re in this amazing bubble and then it’s gone’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Sweden manager Graham Potter tells Lawrence Ostlere about the ‘strange’ emptiness of World Cup elimination, lessons of tournament football and the challenge of building a team to compete with Europe’s best

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

What does it feel like to be knocked out of the World Cup? For weeks you’re inside your own fraternity, a brotherhood going into battle every few days. Then you lose 3-0 to France and it all stops. Cancel the hotels and the flights. No more games, no more training sessions, no more team meetings. One manager recently described the desolation of defeat, wallowing alone in their hotel room as players and staff left for the nearest airport.

“It’s a good description of it,” nods Graham Potter, whose Sweden side were beaten by France this summer in the round of 32. “There’s a week or so where you’re in a bit of an empty state. It’s nothing that I’ve experienced before. For weeks you’re in this amazing bubble where you eat, sleep, drink, work, everything together with these people, and then it’s gone. You don’t know whether that group of people are going to be together again.”

Sweden did have one last evening before they went their separate ways, and they just so happened to be a short ride from Manhattan. “We were in a hotel in New Jersey, so we managed to find our way into New York and had a dinner and a few drinks with the staff, and just enjoyed one night together. And then everybody’s away, and it feels very strange.”

Once the dust had settled, Potter gathered his assistants and analysts to pore over Sweden’s tournament in detail – “a fun part of the job,” he says. Some joined on Zoom calls from their club roles while others met at the Swedish FA headquarters in Stockholm, including the former Sunderland midfielder Seb Larsson, who can often be seen in Potter’s ear. “I haven’t played international football and certainly not for Sweden, and he’s played 130 games, so his experience and understanding of the national team is fantastic,” Potter says.

There were mixed feelings. The World Cup had started perfectly, with a 5-1 win over Tunisia. But a 5-1 defeat by Netherlands and a 1-1 draw with Japan left Sweden third in the group, sending them into the path of the all-powerful French, and they were played off the pitch in New Jersey.

“It’s never nice to lose but sometimes you have to go, ‘OK, maybe the better team won’. But then you have to go, ‘how could we have played better?’ Those thoughts aren’t necessarily in detail on that evening [in Manhattan] but that’s certainly where your brain goes quickly. You have to zoom out and go, ‘OK, we’re disappointed now and it feels really s**t. But would we have taken this when we came in?’ Yeah, of course.”

Potter is meeting The Independent in London in the midst of an impressive Nations League campaign, with Sweden on the verge of promotion to the top tier. He is enjoying the wild ride that has been his first international job, in charge of his adopted country. Potter says he feels Swedish and he sings the national anthem with West Midlands gusto.

It is an unlikely love affair which began when the 35-year-old Potter, who had just graduated from Leeds Metropolitan University with a master’s degree in leadership, took a job no one else wanted in the remote city of Ostersund. The Potters arrived in the depths of winter, when enormous piles of snow line the roads and the sun shines for barely five hours. His wife cried every day for months.

“She’d left her job, her life. It wasn’t like moving to Monaco, especially when you arrive in January, when it’s minus 20-something outside and dark by two o’clock in the afternoon. It’s a wonderful place, but it was tough initially. It’s the fourth tier of Swedish football. So there are times where you’re going, ‘OK, is this right for life and family?’ But you have to give it that time, and thankfully we stuck together and stuck it out, and it was the best thing we’ve ever done. It was worth it.”

After 15 years of highs and lows in the club game, Potter took charge of Sweden last October following a disastrous World Cup qualifying campaign under predecessor Jon Dahl Tomasson. Sweden had one last shot at salvation through the play-offs in March.

He quickly learnt two things about the rhythms of international football. The first is time: enormous gaps of time, yawning canyons of time, almost too much of it. Potter, who owns a house in Sweden but still lives near Brighton, spent the four-month wait for the play-offs flying around Europe meeting his new players. He’d be in the centre of Dortmund one day and the medieval streets of Bergamo the next, then on to London, Liverpool, Newcastle and Glasgow.

“My passport was crammed because you’re just having a half-hour, 40-minute coffee and conversation with players. It’s nice to get a sense of where their careers are at, where their family are at, how they see the situation, because I came into a bad situation. I found it’s very useful to build a relationship, and then it’s very useful to have an understanding of what they’re doing in their clubs.”

Then, suddenly there’s no time at all. The players flew into Valencia for the play-offs on Monday, and on Thursday they played Ukraine in a semi-final. “We had a day and a half [to prepare] and it’s a play-off to go to the World Cup,” Potter says. “So is the game going to be about intricate passes from the back and nice patterns of attacking play? We needed to win two matches. So our starting point was defensive stability, strong in set-pieces and counter-attacking, because we had big-space players like Viktor Gyokeres and Anthony Elanga who are as good as anybody in the world attacking big areas.”

Gyokeres scored a hat-trick to beat Ukraine and then smashed home a dramatic, last-gasp winner to beat Poland and send Sweden to the World Cup, where Potter learnt something else: the brutal finality of tournament football, that shock at a journey ending in the middle.

He spoke to players individually over the summer and found a consensus: they relished the World Cup but left desperate to compete with teams as strong as Netherlands and France. There were signs of life against the Dutch, despite the lopsided scoreline, when Potter changed to a more attacking formation in the first hydration break and Sweden dominated until half-time. The French game, however, was utterly one-sided.

“How do we get to the point where we can beat France? The reality is, if you’re Sweden, you have to have Alex Isak firing off the back of a good season, and probably he wasn’t at that stage. You need Dejan Kulusevski, one of your best players. Isak Hien wasn’t available, our first-choice centre-back. So you want to arrive with the very best that you have.

“The players that we have, when you look at Gyokeres and Isak and Kulusevski and [Yasin] Ayari and [Lucas] Bergvall, there’s a certain profile to them that you have to set up to be proactive against whoever you face, and that’s probably the disappointing thing or the learning point – we weren’t able to do that against France, and if you’re going to lose a game, you’d rather lose in the way we played against the Dutch than how we did against France, even though the scoreline is still painful.

“The players are at a point where they want that type of football. They want to play proactively, they want to play positively, and that’s the exciting challenge.”

There have been signs of evolving into a front-foot team in Sweden’s impressive start to the Nations League, after winning three games and drawing one to take control of Group H with Bosnia, Poland and Romania. Another win over Bosnia on Saturday will seal promotion to League A with Europe’s heavyweights.

Gyokeres has led the charge, scoring in all four Nations League games to take his Sweden record under Potter to 10 goals in 11 matches. He has featured only intermittently for Arsenal this season, but Potter isn’t concerned.

“It doesn’t really matter, is the truth, because he’s done brilliant for us when he’s been playing every week [for Arsenal], and he’s done brilliant for us when he hasn’t been playing every week. Whatever he does in his club, that’s part of the thing that you can’t control. You just have to accept that, and then you just make sure that from a loading perspective, when he comes in you’re careful with him. But he’s such a professional, fit guy that loves playing football for Sweden.”

Kulusevski missed the World Cup through injury but made his long-awaited return to the Tottenham team last month, and Potter sent him a text ahead of the game. “It was just a beautiful moment to see him on the pitch. I’ve not worked with him, that's how long he’s been away, but everybody in the national team says he’s so important, so influential.”

While Kulusevski has been absent, his future brother-in-law has become essential. Yasin Ayari, who is engaged to Kulusevski’s sister Sandra, has been at the heart of Brighton’s flying start to the season and his form for Sweden has been outstanding, with two goals at the World Cup and a starring role in recent Nations League games. “His improvement, I would say from November last year, has been incredible,” beams Potter.

The task now, with Euro 2028 ahead, is to turn Sweden’s most talented group for a generation into a side who can go toe-to-toe with the best teams in the world, to give themselves every chance of staying a little longer before the music stops.

“We all shared the same thing, which was that the World Cup was an amazing experience. But we want to keep going, we want to evolve, we want to improve. It’s not like we’re happy with what we did. We’ve done a lot of good things. The atmosphere in the group was fantastic, amazing, so we took some important steps. But at the same time, you want it to go on. We weren’t ready to go home.”

#997. Mongolia’s iconic grasslands are in crisis — invisible fungi could help save them

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

April Reese is a journalist in Aveiro, Portugal.

More than 70% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, which has implications for the country’s nomadic herders.Credit: Timothy Allen/Getty

Rising temperatures, desertification and overgrazing are taking a heavy toll on Mongolia’s iconic desert grasslands, as well as its nomadic herding culture. But a team of researchers might have hit on an underground solution. They’ve found clues that protecting key fungal networks that support life above the surface could help to preserve biodiversity, boost climate resilience and revive degraded lands.

In most ecosystems, invisible networks of fungi trade resources with plants by interlocking with their roots. These arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi provide the plants with nitrogen and phosphorus gathered from the soil; in return, the plants send excess carbon through their roots to the fungi, helping to sequester it from the atmosphere.

“Mongolia has very unique fungal networks that power these arid grasslands,” says evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers at the Free University of Amsterdam. Kiers is leading a project to map and identify mycorrhizal-fungus hotspots in Mongolia. “As we fight desertification, we want to be able to protect the fungi that are going to be so important for these plants and ecosystems to be restored.”

Working out ways to maintain healthy fungal networks cannot come quickly enough. Around 77% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, and the country is warming three times faster than the global average. Kiers says that paying more attention to fungal networks could help to address the interconnected global challenges of desertification, biodiversity loss and climate change.

It seems that fungi might be starting to get the attention they deserve: last month, at the latest meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, held in Yerevan, Armenia, 3 more countries signed a pledge to conserve fungi, bringing the total number of signatories to 17. And a road map to help countries make good on that pledge, the Global Strategy for Fungal Conservation, was launched.

Kiers’s team is part of the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), a non-profit organization that maps fungal systems around the world and works to protect them. Kiers co-founded the organization in 2021. In September, its researchers announced that they had found more than 500 types of fungus in southwestern Mongolia, 90% of which were previously unknown.

Kiers’s team is in talks with several governments to present its maps of fungal hotspots and data in hopes of supporting the development of strategies to curb desertification and boost climate resilience.

But at the same time as researchers such as Kiers are documenting fungal hotspots, the hotspots might be disappearing. In Mongolia, the team found that degraded land had at least 44% fewer species of mycorrhizal fungi and 60% less plant cover than did non-degraded land.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03589-9

#996. Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay

The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London

Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

#995. How the Man City case could spark a drastic change in English football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Over a third of the league is now up for sale, writes Miguel Delaney, but despite the Man City case, this major shift could bring a solve one of English football’s major problems

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Over the past few weeks, those in Premier League boardrooms have noticed a very distinctive shift.

The previous talk of trying to buy clubs, only for billionaires to realise how few are available, has gradually turned into talk of trying to sell clubs.

The current calculation is that at least eight clubs - over a third of the league - are either officially or unofficially up for sale in some form.

With some of these, there are actual prospectuses. With others, it’s that an ownership would be open to listening to offers. Some would consider full sales, others merely minority stakes.

The current problem, though, is that there are so few buyers.

The market has changed, but it could offer the opportunity for a wider reset.

That may be dependent on a much bigger story, which is a factor in all of this, following the recent developments surrounding the Manchester City case.

Right now, it’s only a few months since another distinctive story - Jeff Bezos’ consortium buying a stake in Liverpool - seemed to mark a high point of high-level purchases.

The Premier League was at that moment seen as a good area to invest due to how it is uncorrelated to global markets, helping to diversify investment portfolios, and this on the back of a boom of US institutional money buying clubs after Covid.

Many of the same factors are now working in reverse.

The great takeover has become the great sell-off. Or, at least, attempted sell-off.

At “absolute level”, one source describes it to The Independent, no one is buying, and there has been “stagnation” in the market.

Some activity still persists at a fractional/minority level but only if it represents real “value”.

Part of it, one experienced source stresses, is “circumstantial”. No deals are going to get through the Independent Football Regulator this side of Christmas, so there is little movement.

Other industry figures stress that billionaires aren’t as willing to invest, due to ongoing global uncertainty. The one tendency is for such billionaires to invest within US sports. Arsenal’s owners, the Kroenke family, struck a deal to buy the Los Angeles Angels for $4bn in September, while Josh Kushner and Bog Iger pulled off a record-breaking $12.5bn deal for the Los Angeles Lakers in August.

The crisis in the Gulf, among other concerns, could affect flow of money in football given how much investment comes from that region. So many corners of the game are now indirectly dependent on it.

The rumours about Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund’s willingness to sell Newcastle United have been swirling for at least two years.

Perhaps most pertinently, though, many buyers see English football as being in an opposite situation to a half-decade ago.

Amid so many takeovers, it was viewed as “a growing trend”, which is generally seen as the best type of business for such investors to get into.

Now, most clubs do not have growing revenues. The English game is seen as having “topped out”.

That could be made clear in the next broadcasting rights cycle, since the last one in the Premier League saw the price per game drop for the first time in the competition’s history.

The current expectation is that domestic rights will stay around the same level and that international rights will marginally drop - unless there’s an unlikely entry from one of the streaming giants.

All of that only deepens the sense that “the Bs” of Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth are excelling, since they all have superb operations and strategy departments.

Few other clubs have that scope for growth.

There’s then that other looming story: City.

A lot of people are waiting to see how that case concludes, especially since it could see the Abu Dhabi ownership sell up, too.

No matter what happens, the very nature of the City story is viewed as inevitably bringing some kind of reset.

Even in the most basic terms, a usually locked-in Champions League place may be opened, and that for a few years. Financial projections can be altered.

Should City unexpectedly prove successful in their appeal, though, they’re back in the centre of all of this and potentially emboldened.

Many prospective ownerships and investors want to see how this lands before acting.

Another layer is if this leads to a forced sale, and potentially a much bigger discussion about state or state-linked ownership.

If such purchases are restricted, it does change the market. Overall ceiling is lowered.

All of this runs alongside a deeper argument that the introduction of the Independent Football Regulator coming in conjunction with the City case offers a rare opportunity for a reset anyway. And not just a reset.

But, given how both developments have involved discussion about core principles of English football, a proper rethink about what the game actually wants to be; what clubs and owners should be; what their role is.

This very increased focus on executives and takeovers only makes clearer the climate we’re in.

English football has gone from the era of the player, up to 1945, through the era of the manager, up to 2003, into the era of the owner. That is to say, the figures that exert the greatest influence on the game.

As the clearest illustration of this, something has obviously gone wrong if a series of clubs with self-sustainably huge fanbases have entire eras completely defined by who their owners happen to be.

In a properly run game, football outlook would be independent of this.

Instead, you only have to look at the examples of Manchester United under the Glazers, Newcastle United under Mike Ashley and arguably his successors, Liverpool under Tom Hicks and George Gillett… and on and on.

The national sport really shouldn’t come down to the pot luck of which of the one per cent picks you, especially when the Independent Football Regulator has specifically recognised the social importance of the game as a matter of law.

That’s also precisely why any future financial regulations shouldn’t be dependent on owner investment, despite so much agitation.

One of the biggest problems in English football right now is a £300m per annum commercial revenue gap between the wealthiest clubs and the rest.

It has been made close to unbridgeable by a system that, as one source tells The Independent, ensures “a hole below the waterline in competitive balance”.

The wage inflation from that similarly drags football’s entire financial system upwards, forcing high-risk capital investment, and creating more and more stress.

That stress has in turn had the effect of ensuring a fan-owned club like AFC Wimbledon have to consider selling off stakes to private investment, despite the Independent Football Regulator expressly encouraging fan ownership.

The system the regulator oversees instead seems to work against that.

It should be a sign, to go with everything else. There has never been a better moment for a reset.

Bosnia-Herzegovina is evolving as a footballing nation, relying on the pull of emotional ties and homeland pride to spearhead their upcoming qualification campaigns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following the retirement of long-time talisman Edin Dzeko, Bosnia-Herzegovina is undergoing a generational shift. Largely, and somewhat uniquely, it is being powered by the emotional pull of a vast global diaspora.

With the domestic league severely underfunded and ill-equipped to serve as a reliable talent conveyor belt for the national team, looking beyond its borders has become a necessity. A series of gifted foreign-born prospects, eligible for their countries of birth yet choosing instead to represent their heritage, is reshaping the team's identity.

At the heart of this recruitment drive is former captain turned sporting director Emir Spahic, who framed the philosophy in late 2024 with a simple declaration: “We’re just bringing our children home.” Having already fielded the third-youngest squad at the 2026 World Cup, this borderless strategy is no longer a temporary stopgap but the blueprint for the nation's footballing future.

A product of Bayer Leverkusen’s academy, Kerim Alajbegovic had a tremendously successful season at Red Bull Salzburg in 2025/2026, registering 14 goals and four assists in 44 competitive appearances in his first season of senior football.

Largely operating on the left flank, Alajbegovic is exceptional in 1-v-1 situations, and is comfortable with both feet. He has begun to hone his game in dead ball situations, developing a signature in-swinging technique on corners from the left, too.

What is striking for a player who only turned 19 in September is that Alajbegovic exudes the confidence of someone who has spent many years playing at the top level, and does not seem phased by the challenges that lie ahead.

His spectacular solo goal against Qatar in Bosnia-Herzegovina’s final group game made him the eighth youngest goalscorer at a World Cup, and the youngest-ever to score from outside the box.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Though Bayer Leverkusen had activated a buy-back clause from Red Bull Salzburg before the tournament, he garnered interest from several top European clubs, before signing for Juventus.

Alajbegovic told Tuttosport that speaking to Miralem Pjanic, a national team legend who spent four trophy-laden seasons in Turin, was an influential factor in his decision.

Alajbegovic’s accomplishments this year were recognised with a place at the Ballon d’Or ceremony, where he was voted 7th in the Men’s Young Talent of the Year award.

Born in Wisconsin in 2005, Esmir Bajraktarevic grew up in a Bosnian household but moved up through the ranks of the game in the USA, establishing himself at New England Revolution in MLS.

After representing the USA at youth level, and gaining one cap at senior level, Bajraktarevic switched to Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a child, he idolised Edin Dzeko, and earlier this year a video of a five-year-old Bajraktarevic wearing a Dzeko top kicking a ball in his back garden went viral. On his international debut against the Netherlands in September 2024, Bajraktarevic set up his boyhood hero with a signature lofted through-ball, and his cinematic rise in the national team was capped off by scoring the deciding penalty kick against Italy to secure Bosnia-Herzegovina’s World Cup qualification.

Bajraktarevic is a left-footed winger operating on the right, who possesses excellent close control and the ability to carve open defences with pinpoint crosses. On his day, he is an electrifying player to watch, whose body feints and mesmerising dinks bring fans out of their seats. Since his move to PSV Eindhoven in January 2025, game-time has sometimes been hard to come by, but this season he has seven goal contributions to his name despite only having 384 Eredivisie minutes under his belt.

Mahmic’s inclusion in Bosnia-Herzegovina’s World Cup squad came as a surprise, given that his impressive performances at Slovan Liberec had gone under the radar in the national media, and he was yet to be capped at senior level.

But the 21-year-old rose to the occasion, scoring a thunderous volley two minutes into his competitive debut versus Switzerland in Los Angeles, before scoring the goal against Qatar that confirmed Bosnia-Herzegovina’s place in the knockout stages of the World Cup. Most frequently deployed in a traditional No. 10 role, Mahmic’s best attributes include his ability to shoot from range and his passing vision, but he also has a knack for popping up in the box to score goals. At six feet tall, Mahmic’s frame enables him to protect the ball effectively when trying to pick out his teammates, too.

On the back of his eye-catching World Cup performances, Mahmic was signed by Corum, an ambitious, newly-promoted club in the Turkish Super Lig, for the second-highest transfer fee in the club’s history. He then scored on his debut against Besiktas and contributed regularly in the final third despite limited time on the pitch.

Nadan Hadzic is a Sarajevo-born freelance journalist based in London. His work has been featured in publications such as The Observer, Sports Politika and The World Today. He has been a guest on podcasts and radio programmes to discuss Balkans football. He was shortlisted in the Academy category of the 2024 British Sports Journalism Awards.

#992. A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?

It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma

By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them.

And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings.

Yet, apparently, a crisis of a sort has been churning just below the surface of what is, by broad consensus, Europe’s best home support.

On Friday, Dortmund had announced a kind of bribery scheme. A rewards program is probably a kinder way of putting it. Fans who stayed off their phones during the bout with Eintracht had the chance to win signed jerseys and earn gift cards to the club’s merchandise store. If they activated a so-called “fan mode” on the club’s app – a name so phenomenally passive-aggressive you can only applaud whoever came up with it – the club could count who unlocked their phones the fewest times during the game. For every minute the fans left their phones alone, they got points.

Dortmund are not the only German team to pick a fight with phones.

Second-division clubs Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden have banned commercial influencer-style videos in their stadiums altogether, fearing for both the integrity of the TV rights they sell and the experience of their fans. Dortmund, likewise, appear motivated by the incursion of influencers, who are siphoning off and monetizing footage of the famous match-day experience and growing into a nuisance for regulars.

This problem has also afflicted the tennis majors. The US Open now resembles an influencer convention more than it does a tennis tournament. When the US Tennis Association credentialed more than 100 content creators this year, the influencers grew so disruptive that a match was stopped when a chair umpire had to ask them to turn off a ring light. Wimbledon has refused to credential influencers for just this reason, which doesn’t stop them from getting in with regular tickets or through sponsors.

Dortmund’s attempt at shaping fan behavior, however, goes further than warding off the cultural content parasites. This please-stop-holding-up-your-phones-and-just-live-in-the-present plea raises quasi-existential questions about sport and its consumption.

“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramer said. “And that’s exactly what we’re putting front and center together.”

“Anyone at a soccer game should experience the moment and the emotions – not just a cell phone screen,” added Marcel de Groot, the chief executive of Vodafone Germany, both a cellphone service provider and a Dortmund sponsor. “Let’s leave our smartphones in our pockets more often at the stadium and instead focus on what’s happening on the field and in the stands.”

These were statements delivered with unshakeable confidence in their righteousness, yet there is evidence to suggest this simply isn’t how some fans want to behave at stadiums.

Which begs the question: can, and should, professional sports teams get to dictate how their ticket-buying fans experience their games? It’s surely a question that’s crossed the mind of all the musicians who now perform to a sea of cell phones, their flashlights on, obscuring the faces in the crowd. Did their fans buy the right to experience the concert as they please? Or does this objectify the musicians and diminish the performance, somehow?

It goes back to the question of whether sport is entertainment, and whether its consumers get to sit back and let the proceedings and the attendant stimuli wash over them. Or whether they are something else entirely: active participants in the games they attend. If that is so, then fandom amounts to a parasocial relationship conferring membership to a community with attendant behavioral expectations.

What are the responsibilities of the ticketholder? Do teams get to purity-test their supporters? What do fans owe their teams? Is live soccer just content? A day out, not unlike going to the movies or a museum, where nobody expects total focus and for you to cheer on the thing you’re looking at? Is it heresy to even suggest this?

The latter tends to be the view, or at least the vibe, in most American sports leagues where fans are often less engaged, told by an announcer and a jumbo screen when and what to clap or stomp or chant. This has always contrasted with the feel of global football, where the folklore is usually organic, sparked and dictated by the fans themselves. It’s why all of those pre-game and half-time concerts at the World Cup final rankled, drowning out the thrum of the throaty Argentina fans.

It feels both instructive and fitting that this debate broke out at Dortmund. The Bundesliga’s rules on safeguarding fan majority ownership of very nearly every club have preserved the league as a kind of supporters’ paradise, with relatively cheap tickets and policies that put fans first. Dortmund, for their part, have been held up for years as a paradigm for their following – thus attracting the influencers, of course.

The latter will be dealt with, it seems. In an age when soccer clubs are essentially production houses who also field company teams, it always seemed inevitable that these interlopers would be expelled from the premises. The fans, however, are not so easily corrected on behavior their teams have deemed undesirable. And they will vote with their credit cards.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#991. Beloved football broadcaster Danny Kelly dies aged 69

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Widely popular on radio, with a long spell at talkSport, Kelly, a lifelong Tottenham fan, confirmed he was diagnosed with oesophageal cancer earlier this year

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The popular sports broadcaster Danny Kelly has died aged 69 after a battle with cancer.

A lifelong Tottenham fan, but beloved by fans from all clubs, Kelly announced earlier this year that he had been diagnosed with oesophageal cancer.

Kelly featured on popular shows Kick Off, Sporting Life and Trans-Euro Express, while also becoming a major part of The Athletic’s Tottenham podcast The View From The Lane as its presenter. Kelly was also a music lover and spent two years as editor of the NME.

And the football community is mourning the loss of the beloved presenter, with talkSPORT paying tribute to Kelly and sharing one of his most iconic quotes on air: “I love football, Stan. I love it.”

The broadcaster added that Kelly was “a cherished part of talkSPORT for so many years” and brought “extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves. His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.”

Tottenham paid tribute to their famous supporter, stating: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Danny.”

Kelly, who had moved to Ireland, announced he was stepping away from broadcasting in March and encouraged listeners to get checked. His passing has prompted a flood of tributes, including his long-time broadcasting partner Danny Baker, who said: “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon. I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

While former Crystal Palace owner, talkSPORT pundit and friend Simon Jordan said: "He was a brilliant broadcaster, editor, writer and friend, the reason I'm able to broadcast is because of Danny, it started with Danny, he nurtured me. He was an ideas factory. He fought this battle, the adversity he went through, the sadness, I feel choked, we thought Danny was coming through. He showed such strength and courage.

“We had such fun, during Covid we had such little material, nothing was going on, we had ideological debates, we disagreed, but we still created a dynamic between us, it’s stayed with me. I know him from years back. He will be missed, by those who knew him, the way he’d tell stories, strong views.”

talkSPORT colleague Ian ‘Moose’ Abrahams added: “Absolutely heartbroken to hear Danny Kelly has passed away. One of the best broadcasters I’ve worked with. One of the most amazing, kindest, funny, passionate people I knew. Danny, we’ll always have “I love Football”. I will miss you my friend, sleep well.”

Another colleague and former Liverpool, Tottenham and England midfielder Danny Murphy said: "The warmth and the humour, the knowledge, I thought, 'I'd bring up a song I like from the 60s and 70s, try catch him out', every time he would say, 'I met him,' I'd always laugh with him."

Broadcaster Laura Woods said: “I felt so sad, I had so many great memories with him, he was a guidance to me. We had production meetings, sitting around Danny, it was like kids at school, great stories. The level of knowledge he had, about anything and everything. He was so pure and genuine, that’s so unique.

“He would say it how it was, I loved that, I was in awe of him. He challenged me, in the right way, very gentle and kind, interesting. He’d give you so much knowledge, I credit him with my early development, I will miss him.”

#988. England's best? Record-breaking Ballon d'Or winner Kane set for Wembley celebration

England captain Harry Kane set to win record-breaking 126th England cap in Nations League this week; Kane was voted England's greatest in a Sky Sports poll - but biggest prize still awaits; follow England vs Croatia with the Sky Sports website and app on Thursday; kick-off 7.45pm

Senior Football Journalist @psmithXI

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Harry Kane is set to become England's most-capped player ever on Thursday night - will it also be time to crown him the country's greatest?

Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph last month coronated him as the world's best for the past year. Whether he should have the all-time No 1 spot for his country makes for a fascinating debate - not least with the weight of a World Cup win on the side of historic icons such as Bobby Charlton (another Ballon d'Or winner) and Bobby Moore (another captain fantastic).

But, minus the big team triumph, Kane's individual case is compelling.

Interestingly, Sky Sports readers went for Kane when we asked the question following his 125th cap for the Three Lions in October. Kane took 49 per cent of the vote from almost 100,000 respondents.

A major-tournament win would surely take him into undisputed territory. Cruelly, through two European Championship finals - including one settled on penalties at Wembley - and two World Cup semi-final heartaches, that international trophy currently remains elusive.

After ending his club trophy wait with his move to Bayern Munich, Kane would dearly love the latter years of his career to also bring England success. Perhaps the Nations League is where he and his team-mates will break that long wait for silverware? England are almost certain of a place in March's quarter-finals and can make a statement against Croatia and Spain this week.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

But even without the big England win, Kane's huge goal haul, consistency, leadership and multi-faceted quality put him on a pedestal. He is guaranteed a fitting show of respect and admiration for all of that ahead of kick-off with Croatia.

Kane is almost certain to start that fixture, meaning he will go to 126 appearances for his country, one more than legendary goalkeeper Peter Shilton.

International games come more frequently these days, of course, but Kane's relentlessness is well worthy of celebration. He's always hungry to get onto the pitch and go for goals and that's reflected in his stats. He has been unavailable for just one of the past 101 competitive matches England have played, a defeat to Greece in 2024 in the Nations League.

Inevitably there have been highs and lows - and plenty of criticism to ride through before what is likely to be a night of tribute this week.

The agonising campaign to add to that World Cup win of Moore, Charlton and co goes on but in the Kane era, England have never gone closer. From going to the final four in 2018 in Russia to the painful turnaround loss to Argentina in the USA which ultimately led to a third-place World Cup finish, Kane has been a central figure.

There have been moments when he has been fiercely scrutinised, particularly in summers when it appeared he was worn out by the rigours of the previous season.

There have been big misses - from close range against Croatia in that World Cup semi-final, for instance, or his second penalty against France at the 2022 World Cup, when he skied the ball off target when he looked primed to take the quarter-final to extra-time.

But mainly there have been goals. So many goals. For years, Charlton's total of 49 was the record total for an England player. Wayne Rooney just managed to overhaul it at the end of his career, lifting the bar to 53. Kane has smashed it. He's up to 91 and counting, as prolific as he's ever been.

On the occasion of his 125th cap against the Czech Republic, he added two more to his total. A Croatia side who he also struck twice against in that incredible 7-0 victory in October will be fearing more punishment from the England skipper.

With a long-coveted Ballon d'Or in his possession, Kane appears to be at the peak of his powers: the goal machine who can also set up opportunities for others and make the play from deep. An all-round superstar.

On Thursday, those stratospheric heights he's reached will be recognised. But be sure, Kane - along with England supporters - will be wondering whether he and this team can go even higher for the truly magnificent prizes they all crave.

Follow England vs Croatia with the Sky Sports website and App on Thursday; kick-off 7.45pm

Michael Carrick’s future as Manchester United manager is in severe doubt after overseeing the club’s worst start to the Premier League season in 40 years and with his side in the relegation zone.

A second Old Trafford comeback of the week, this time battling from two goals down twice to rescue a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday, might not be enough to save Carrick’s job and he is at risk of being sacked after just 10 games of the season and with his side 18th during the international break.

United ended a nine-game winless run when they came from two goals down to beat Roma in the Champions League last week but they have not won in eight attempts in the Premier League and have just one top-flight win this campaign.

Carrick survived crisis talks with the United hierarchy after defeats to Como and Bournemouth last month and was given time to turn results around, but speculation over a change begun the day after Sunday’s chaotic draw and The Independent understands contact was made with United States boss Mauricio Pochettino over succeeding Carrick.

Manchester United have made their worst start to a season in 40 years under Michael Carrick this year.

They’ve won just once in the Premier League, against Ipswich Town, and have gained only eight points from the first 10 matches.

Pressure has mounted increasingly on Carrick over recent weeks though United are unbeaten in their last two games with a 3-2 win over Roma in the Champions League followed by a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on Sunday.

That win over Roma is United’s only victory, across all competitions, in their last 11 games.

United’s recent ramshackle play has left them in the Premier League relegation zone and provided no definitive answer on Carrick’s capability, leaving the club’s decision makers with a big choice.

With the decision over Carrick’s future to be made in Monaco, the current United manager has arrived at the Carrington training ground to continue on as normal.

With the international break now in full flow, Carrick is taking training with the members of United’s squad not chosen to for international duty.

Carrick’s handling of the situation and speculation has been admired but, like all of us, he is waiting for an update on his situation.

Manchester United have opened talks with USMNT boss Mauricio Pochettino as they explore their options to replace Michael Carrick.

Pochettino and the club are reportedly ‘close’ to agreeing a deal after talks on Tuesday between United and representatives for the Argentine.

According to The Athletic, no issues over personal terms are anticipated but United would have to trigger an exit clause in Pochettino’s US Soccer contract which is worth $10m (£7.4m).

Securing Pochettino services would also come with the additional expense of compensation for his staff who will join him at Old Trafford.

Let’s run down where things are currently at in regards to Michael Carrick’s future at Manchester United.

No decision over his future has yet been made but signs are pointing to the current boss facing the sack as early as today.

Carrick’s United have struggled this season with only one win in the Premier League and the team sitting 18th in the table after 10 games.

The powers that be at Old Trafford are set to meet today in Monaco to discuss the next steps for the club with those discussions set to revolve around the future of Carrick as manager.

The Manchester United fans have been vocal in support of Carrick, especially in the wake of a comeback victory over Roma last week and another comeback to draw 4-4 with Aston Villa in the league on Sunday.

United are also reportedly undergoing due diligence on possible replacements for Carrick with Mauricio Pochettino currently the favourite to step into the dugout if Carrick is sacked.

It could be a day of movement for Manchester United as the club’s hierarchy are set to meet in Monaco to discuss the future of manager Michael Carrick.

#986. How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay

Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League

I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.

Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.

This passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.

Now the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.

Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.

There have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking: “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”

Football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have said, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.

This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.

At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?

Again, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.

The first issue is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.

And maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.

This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

If you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary issue derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.

What are the consequences of this new fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.

And here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.

Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to issues of personal principle.

The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?

There are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.

This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest issue here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been said out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.
